name: Transfer Pricing
title: Transfer Pricing
answer: Transfer pricing is the set of rules and practices for setting and testing the prices charged in transactions between related entities that operate in different tax jurisdictions. It covers sales of goods, provision of services, licensing of intangibles, intercompany financing, and cost sharing arrangements. The work also includes allocating profits and losses among group members so that each jurisdiction receives an arm's length return. In practice, the scope reaches from routine distribution and manufacturing to complex intellectual property and financial transactions.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Transfer pricing is the set of rules and practices for setting and testing the prices charged in transactions between related entities that operate in different tax jurisdictions. It covers sales of goods, provision of services, licensing of intangibles, intercompany financing, and cost sharing arrangements. The work also includes allocating profits and losses among group members so that each jurisdiction receives an arm's length return. In practice, the scope reaches from routine distribution and manufacturing to complex intellectual property and financial transactions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on financial and operational data drawn from enterprise resource planning systems, legal entity ledgers, intercompany agreements, and transfer pricing policies. It also depends on external benchmarking databases and public filings that provide comparables for prices and margins. Tax authority guidance, such as the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines and local regulations, sets the analytical framework. Version controlled documentation and audit trails are essential because the same numbers must be defended across multiple jurisdictions.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is a functional analysis that identifies what each related party does, what assets it uses, and what risks it assumes. From that analysis, the tax team selects the most appropriate transfer pricing method, such as the comparable uncontrolled price method, the resale price method, the cost plus method, the transactional net margin method, or the profit split method. Benchmarking studies then search for comparable transactions or companies to support an arm's length result. The output is a set of intercompany agreements, pricing policies, and local files or master files that document the position.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Transfer pricing carries significant risk of double taxation, penalties, and adjustments if a tax authority disagrees with the pricing or the documentation. Provenance matters because every figure in a benchmarking study or financial model must trace back to a source system, a contract, or a public database. Legal privilege and confidentiality rules shape what can be shared with auditors and what must be protected. Governance also requires clear ownership of the transfer pricing policy, regular reviews, and consistent application across entities.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more automated data pipelines that pull intercompany transactions directly from accounting systems and flag outliers for review. Artificial intelligence is being applied to contract analysis, comparables selection, and risk scoring, though human judgment remains central to functional analysis and method selection. Greater transparency through country by country reporting and multilateral tax reforms is pushing groups to maintain real time, defensible positions. The direction is toward continuous compliance rather than an annual documentation exercise.
